tspan.tspan: The Lighthouse Keeper's Ledger
Every evening at dusk the keeper climbed the one hundred and twelve steps of the tower,
wound the clockwork that turned the great lens, and wrote a single line in the ledger. Over
forty years the ledger filled eleven volumes, and nearly every line recorded the same three
facts: the time the lamp was lit, the direction of the wind, and the number of ships that
passed before midnight.
Historians who later studied the ledgers found that the plain entries told a richer story than
anyone expected. Long gaps between ships marked the winters when the northern harbour
froze. A sudden rise in traffic matched the year a canal opened two hundred miles inland.
Even the handwriting changed, growing smaller and more careful after the storm that
destroyed the old pier.
The keeper never described the storm itself. The entry for that night reads only that the lamp
was lit at seven minutes past five, that the wind blew from the south-west, and that no ships
passed. The next morning, according to the harbour records, fishermen found the lantern
room glass cracked in four places, yet the light had not gone out once during the night.
Today the tower is automated, and the ledgers rest in a climate-controlled archive beside
navigation charts from the same decades. Researchers compare the two sources to estimate
how shipping routes shifted as engines replaced sails. Their work depends on a simple
practice repeated without fail: a person who wrote down what they saw, every single day,
whether or not anything seemed to happen.
Visitors who reach the top of the tower can still read a copy of the first entry, framed beside
the lens. It notes a calm sea, a light westerly breeze, and three fishing boats returning late
with full nets.
